questions.title: Characteristic feature of the pars nervosa
questions.question: The following is a characteristic feature of the pars nervosa:

options.A: It is formed of groups of nerve cells separated by fenestrated capillaries.
options.B: It has accumulated neurosecretion called Herring bodies.
options.C: It is formed of follicles of basophilic cells with granular cytoplasm.
options.D: It has an upward extension known as the pars tuberalis.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pars nervosa contains few or no nerve cell bodies; it is made mainly of unmyelinated axons of hypothalamic magnocellular neurons and supporting pituicytes, not groups of nerve cells around fenestrated capillaries.
explanations.B: Correct. The pars nervosa (posterior pituitary) is the storage and release site for hypothalamic hormones, and the axons reaching it show dilated terminals packed with neurosecretory granules. These accumulations are visible by light microscopy as Herring bodies. They store oxytocin or ADH bound to neurophysin, awaiting release into the fenestrated capillaries of the neurohypophysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Follicles of basophilic cells with granular cytoplasm describe glandular adenohypophyseal tissue, not the pars nervosa, which contains no follicles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pars tuberalis is an upward extension of the pars distalis (adenohypophysis) around the infundibular stalk, not of the pars nervosa.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise Herring bodies as the characteristic accumulated neurosecretion of the pars nervosa.

questions.title: Stain that identifies mammotrophs
questions.question: Mammotrophs could be identified by the following stain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Silver stains demonstrate reticular fibres and argyrophil cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system, not pituitary mammotrophs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orcein is an elastic-fibre stain and is not used to demonstrate the acidophilic mammotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orange G selectively stains the somatotrophs (growth-hormone acidophils), not the prolactin-secreting mammotrophs.
explanations.D: Correct. Mammotrophs (lactotrophs) are the prolactin-secreting acidophils of the pars distalis, and among the acidophils they are demonstrated with carmine (erythrosin or carmine), which distinguishes them from the orange-G-positive somatotrophs. This selective affinity lets the two acidophil populations be told apart in stained sections. Their number and granularity increase markedly during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify carmine as the selective stain for prolactin-secreting mammotrophs, distinct from orange-G somatotrophs.

questions.title: Common feature of the diffuse neuroendocrine system
questions.question: A common feature of the cells of the diffuse neuro-endocrine system (DNES) is that they:

options.C: Are rich in sER and lysosomes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNES cells arise from several germ layers, many from neural crest and neuroectoderm as well as endoderm, so a single endodermal origin is not their common feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNES cells are defined by abundant membrane-bound dense-core secretory granules storing peptides and amines, so being granule-free is the opposite of the truth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. They are not characterised chiefly by smooth ER and lysosomes; their hallmark is amine-precursor uptake and decarboxylation with dense-core granule storage.
explanations.D: Correct. The diffuse neuroendocrine system (formerly called APUD) is a scattered population of amine- and peptide-secreting cells that share key properties with neurons: they take up amine precursors, decarboxylate them, and store the products in dense-core granules for regulated release. Because of this shared biochemistry and secretory behaviour they are regarded as highly modified neurons. Many indeed derive from the neural crest.

questions.learning_objective: State that DNES cells behave as highly modified neurons sharing the amine-handling and granule-storage properties of neurons.

questions.title: Development of the pituitary gland
questions.question: Regarding the development of the pituitary gland, mark the one correct statement:

options.A: The infundibulum arises as a mesodermal diverticulum from the roof of the diencephalon.
options.B: The infundibulum forms the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland.
options.C: Rathke's pouch is an endodermal diverticulum from the floor of the stomodeum.
options.D: It is derived from two sources: the infundibulum and Rathke's pouch.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The infundibulum is a neuroectodermal, not mesodermal, downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon, so both the germ layer and the site are wrong here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The infundibulum forms the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) and stalk, not the anterior lobe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal diverticulum from the roof of the stomodeum (primitive mouth), not an endodermal outgrowth from its floor.
explanations.D: Correct. The hypophysis has a dual origin: an ectodermal outpocketing of the stomodeal roof (Rathke's pouch) forms the adenohypophysis (anterior lobe, pars intermedia and pars tuberalis), while a neuroectodermal downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon (the infundibulum) forms the neurohypophysis (posterior lobe and stalk). These two primordia meet and fuse to build the definitive gland. This is why the pituitary has both a glandular and a neural part.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the dual embryological origin of the pituitary from Rathke's pouch and the infundibulum.

questions.title: Cells spared in cryptorchidism
questions.question: In cryptorchidism (undescended testes), the following cells are not affected:
questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary spermatocytes belong to the temperature-sensitive germ-cell line and are damaged when the testis remains at core body temperature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spermatids are late germ cells and are among the first to be lost when spermatogenesis fails in an undescended testis.
explanations.C: Correct. In cryptorchidism the seminiferous (germinal) epithelium is exposed to the higher intra-abdominal temperature, which arrests and destroys the temperature-sensitive spermatogenic cells. The interstitial Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone, are relatively resistant to this heat and are spared, so androgen production and secondary sexual characters are usually preserved. This is why an untreated undescended testis causes infertility but not necessarily hypoandrogenism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secondary spermatocytes are germ cells formed during meiosis and are also lost when the heat-sensitive spermatogenic line is damaged.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that cryptorchidism damages heat-sensitive germ cells while sparing the interstitial Leydig cells.

questions.title: Least likely effect of chronic androgen abuse
questions.question: Chronic androgen abuse by healthy male athletes is least likely to result in:
questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. Androgens stimulate renal erythropoietin and the bone marrow, so chronic abuse tends to raise the red-cell mass, making increased erythropoiesis an expected effect.
explanations.B: Correct. Exogenous androgens suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis by negative feedback, lowering GnRH and therefore LH and FSH. Without adequate intratesticular testosterone and FSH support, spermatogenesis declines and the sperm count falls rather than rises. This is why anabolic-steroid abuse is a recognised cause of male infertility and testicular atrophy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By raising haemoglobin and muscle mass, androgen abuse can improve physical endurance, so a rise in endurance is an expected rather than a least-likely result.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The classic sought-after effect of androgen abuse is anabolic growth of skeletal muscle, so increased muscle mass is expected.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that exogenous androgens suppress the HPG axis and reduce sperm count despite their anabolic effects.

questions.title: Ovarian hilar cells
questions.question: Concerning the ovarian hilar cells, they:

options.A: Are located in the ovarian cortex.
options.B: Are structurally related to Sertoli cells.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hilar cells lie in the ovarian hilum, the medulla/hilus region where vessels enter, not in the cortex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hilar cells are the ovarian counterpart of the testicular interstitial (Leydig) cells, not of Sertoli cells.
explanations.C: Correct. Ovarian hilar cells are steroidogenic cells in the hilum that are homologous to testicular Leydig cells, and like Leydig cells they contain rod-shaped cytoplasmic Reinke's crystalloids. They secrete androgens, and their hyperplasia or tumours can cause virilisation. Their presence and crystalloids are the histological clue to their Leydig-cell nature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hilar cells secrete androgens like Leydig cells; progesterone is the product of the corpus luteum granulosa-lutein cells, not of hilar cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ovarian hilar cells as Leydig-cell homologues containing Reinke's crystalloids and secreting androgens.

questions.title: Function of the syncytiotrophoblast
questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding the syncytiotrophoblast:

options.A: It is responsible for the secretion of placental hormones.
options.B: It is formed of pale-stained cells.
options.D: It disappears after the 4th month of pregnancy.

questions.subject: obs

explanations.A: Correct. The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer of the placental villus in direct contact with maternal blood, and it is the main endocrine tissue of the placenta. It synthesises and secretes the placental hormones, including human chorionic gonadotropin, human placental lactogen, progesterone and estrogens. It also carries out maternofetal exchange across its microvillous surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast has darkly stained, densely packed nuclei and cytoplasm; it is the underlying cytotrophoblast (Langhans cells) that appears pale.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Its maternal-facing surface bears abundant microvilli, a brush border that greatly increases the area for exchange, so it is not devoid of microvilli.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast persists throughout pregnancy as the exchange and endocrine surface; it is the cytotrophoblast that becomes discontinuous in later pregnancy.

questions.learning_objective: State that the syncytiotrophoblast is the endocrine layer of the placenta secreting hCG, hPL and steroid hormones.

questions.title: Lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa
questions.question: The lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa is formed by:

options.D: The obturator internus muscle and its fascia.

questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The levator ani with its fascia forms the sloping medial wall and roof of the ischiorectal fossa, not the lateral wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external anal sphincter lies medially around the anal canal, contributing to the medial wall, not the lateral wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the bowel's own circular muscle around the anal canal and is not a wall of the ischiorectal fossa.
explanations.D: Correct. The ischiorectal (ischio-anal) fossa is a wedge-shaped space lateral to the anal canal, and its lateral wall is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by its fascia, together with the lower part of the ischial tuberosity. The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal), carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels, runs within this fascia on the lateral wall. The medial wall, by contrast, is the levator ani and the external anal sphincter.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the obturator internus and its fascia as the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa carrying the pudendal canal.

questions.title: What the pelvic diaphragm separates
questions.question: The pelvic diaphragm separates the:

options.A: True pelvis from the false pelvis.
options.C: Deep perineal pouch from the superficial perineal pouch.

questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The true pelvis is separated from the false pelvis by the pelvic brim (inlet), not by the pelvic diaphragm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ischiorectal fossa lies within the perineum below the pelvic diaphragm; the diaphragm does not separate the perineum from that fossa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The deep and superficial perineal pouches are separated from each other by the perineal membrane, not by the pelvic diaphragm.
explanations.D: Correct. The pelvic diaphragm, formed by the levator ani and coccygeus muscles with their fasciae, is the muscular floor of the pelvic cavity. It separates the pelvic cavity above from the perineum below. Structures such as the anal canal and the urethra pass through it to reach the perineum.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pelvic diaphragm separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum.

questions.title: Ligament of the ovary
questions.question: Which of the following is a ligament of the ovary?
questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Correct. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) is a peritoneal fold that attaches the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and transmits the ovarian vessels, nerves and lymphatics. It is a true ligament of the ovary, along with the ligament of the ovary proper and the mesovarium. It is ligated when removing the ovary because it carries the ovarian artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The utero-vesical fold is a peritoneal reflection between the uterus and bladder; it is not a ligament of the ovary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no named utero-rectal ligament of the ovary; the recto-uterine (uterosacral) folds relate the cervix to the sacrum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The broad ligament is a ligament of the uterus that encloses the tube and suspends the ovary through the mesovarium, but it is not itself the ovarian ligament.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the suspensory ligament as a true ligament of the ovary transmitting the ovarian vessels.

questions.title: Origin of the ovarian arteries
questions.question: The ovarian arteries originate from:

options.B: The abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries.
options.C: The abdominal aorta above the renal arteries.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ovarian arteries do not arise from the renal arteries, which supply the kidneys.
explanations.B: Correct. The ovarian arteries arise directly from the front of the abdominal aorta a short distance below the origin of the renal arteries, at about the level of L2. They descend retroperitoneally and reach the ovary through the suspensory ligament. Their high origin reflects the ovary's development high on the posterior abdominal wall before its descent into the pelvis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ovarian arteries arise below, not above, the renal arteries.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal iliac artery supplies the uterus through the uterine artery and much of the pelvis, but the ovarian artery comes from the aorta, not the internal iliac.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries.

questions.title: Part of the broad ligament supporting the uterine tube
questions.question: The part of the broad ligament giving attachment and support to the uterine tube is called the:
questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mesometrium is the largest part of the broad ligament below the mesovarium, related to the body of the uterus, not to the tube.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesovarium is the short posterior fold that suspends the ovary, not the uterine tube.
explanations.C: Correct. The mesosalpinx is the upper free part of the broad ligament lying between the uterine (fallopian) tube above and the ovary and mesovarium below. It encloses and supports the uterine tube and contains the epoophoron and the anastomosing tubal branches of the ovarian and uterine vessels. Salpinx means tube, which is the clue to its name.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The round ligament of the uterus runs from the uterine cornu to the labium majus through the inguinal canal; it is not a supporting mesentery of the tube.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mesosalpinx as the part of the broad ligament enclosing and supporting the uterine tube.

questions.title: Hormones derived from tyrosine
questions.question: Which of the following hormones are derived from one amino acid (tyrosine)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cortisol is a steroid hormone synthesised from cholesterol, not from an amino acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid steroid derived from cholesterol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Parathyroid hormone is a polypeptide of 84 amino acids, not a single-amino-acid derivative.
explanations.D: Correct. The thyroid hormones T3 and T4 are amine hormones synthesised from the amino acid tyrosine, which is iodinated and coupled within thyroglobulin. The catecholamines are also tyrosine derivatives, so tyrosine is the shared precursor of this amine class. This distinguishes thyroid hormones from the steroid (cholesterol-derived) and peptide hormones.

questions.learning_objective: Classify thyroid hormones as amine hormones derived from the amino acid tyrosine.

questions.title: G protein-linked hormone receptors
questions.question: Which of the following is correct as regards the G protein-linked hormone receptors?

options.A: In the active state, the alpha subunit bound to GTP dissociates from the G protein.
options.B: They are activated by steroid hormones to increase the enzyme activity of protein synthesis.
options.C: They are proteins that pass the membrane only once and function directly as enzymes.
options.D: In the active state, the beta subunit dissociates from the beta-gamma complex to associate with other signalling proteins.

explanations.A: Correct. When an agonist binds a G-protein-coupled receptor, the receptor catalyses exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein. The GTP-bound alpha subunit then dissociates from the beta-gamma dimer and goes on to regulate effector enzymes such as adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C. Hydrolysis of GTP back to GDP terminates the signal and lets the subunits reassociate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Steroid hormones act on intracellular nuclear receptors, not on membrane G-protein-coupled receptors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GPCRs are seven-transmembrane (serpentine) proteins that signal through a G protein; single-pass receptors that are themselves enzymes describe the catalytic receptor-tyrosine-kinase class.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the alpha subunit bound to GTP that dissociates from the beta-gamma complex to signal; the beta-gamma dimer stays together.

questions.learning_objective: Describe activation of a GPCR by dissociation of the GTP-bound alpha subunit from the beta-gamma dimer.

questions.title: Site of 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol
questions.question: The site of 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The kidney performs the second, 1-alpha-hydroxylation step that yields the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, not the 25-hydroxylation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The skin is where 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) by ultraviolet light, before any hydroxylation.
explanations.C: Correct. Cholecalciferol undergoes its first hydroxylation at carbon 25 in the liver, producing 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form. This step is not tightly regulated, so plasma 25-OH-D reflects vitamin D status. The subsequent 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney is the regulated, activating step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lung has no role in vitamin D hydroxylation.

questions.module_subject: 207 END > Physiology > Calcium and vitamin D
questions.learning_objective: State that 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol occurs in the liver, forming calcidiol.

questions.title: Active form of vitamin D
questions.question: The active form of vitamin D is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) is the inactive precursor formed in the skin; it must be hydroxylated twice to become active.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is generally regarded as an inactive degradation metabolite, not the active hormone.
explanations.C: Correct. The biologically active form of vitamin D is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), produced by 1-alpha-hydroxylation of the 25-OH precursor in the kidney. It acts on intestine, bone and kidney to raise plasma calcium and phosphate. Its formation is stimulated by parathyroid hormone and by low plasma phosphate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) is the major circulating form but is only weakly active; it is the substrate for renal activation.

questions.module_subject: 207 END > Physiology > Calcium and vitamin D
questions.learning_objective: Identify 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) as the active hormonal form of vitamin D.

questions.title: Pancreatic cells secreting glucagon
questions.question: Glucagon is secreted by which cells of the pancreas?

explanations.A: Correct. Glucagon is secreted by the alpha (A) cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. These cells respond to hypoglycaemia by releasing glucagon, which raises blood glucose through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In the human islet they lie mainly at the periphery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta cells secrete insulin, together with amylin and C-peptide, not glucagon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. G cells secrete gastrin and are found mainly in the gastric antrum; they are not the islet source of glucagon.

questions.learning_objective: State that pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon.
